H1.text: A lamp hangs still. A tug of war rope stops dead. A bridge holds up a bus.

H2.text: Big forces act on all three. So why does nothing move?

H3.text: Aarav ties a rope across his study window, and hangs his two kilogram bag in the middle.

H4.text: The rope sags. He pulls it tighter, and tighter. Still it sags. Why can it never go straight?

P1.text: A body is in equilibrium when the net force on it is zero. All its forces, with their directions, cancel out.

P3.text: Then there is no acceleration. It stays at rest, or moves at a steady velocity.

P4.text: The simplest case: a lamp on one cord.

P5.text: Its weight pulls down. The cord pulls up. That pull is called tension.

P6.text: They must be equal, opposite, and on one line. So the tension equals the weight.

S1.text: Now Aarav's bag. Two strings, each at an angle theta to the horizontal.

S2.text: At sixty degrees, each string pulls with eleven point three newtons. The bag weighs nineteen point six.

S3.text: Pull them flatter. At thirty degrees, each tension is nineteen point six. The whole weight.

S4.text: At ten degrees, fifty six newtons. At five, over one hundred and twelve. On the graph, the tension shoots up.

S6.text: Slow-mo replay. Freeze, and split each tension into two parts.

S7.text: The sideways parts are big, but equal and opposite. They cancel.

S8.text: The upward parts are tiny, yet together they must hold the whole weight.

D1.text: Now the rule, one step at a time.

D2.text: Step one. Equilibrium: the net force is zero. Sigma F equals zero.

D3.text: Step two. In each direction: sigma F x is zero, and sigma F y is zero.

D4.text: Step three. Sideways: T one cos theta equals T two cos theta. So both tensions are equal. Call them T.

D5.text: Step four. Upward: two T sine theta equals the weight, W.

D6.text: Step five. So T equals W over two sine theta.

T1.text: Remember this. In equilibrium, the forces in every direction add up to zero.

R1.text: Now, back to Aarav's rope. Link by link.

R2.text: Flatter strings mean a smaller angle theta, so a smaller sine theta.

R3.text: So each string gives a smaller upward part. To hold the weight, the tension must grow.

R5.text: At zero degrees, sine theta is zero. No upward part, so no tension is enough. The rope can never go perfectly straight.

K1.text: Side by side. Two forces: the lamp. Equal, opposite, on one line.

K2.text: Three forces: the bag at thirty degrees, all nineteen point six newtons. Tip to tail, they close into a triangle.

K3.text: The triangle closes, so the net force is zero.

K4.text: Now you try. Can forces of three, four and nine newtons keep a ring in equilibrium? Pause and decide.

K5.text: No! Three plus four is only seven. It can never reach nine, so the triangle cannot close.

V1.text: Another pair. A raindrop falls at a steady speed. Drag balances its weight. It moves, yet it is in equilibrium.

V2.text: A ball thrown up stops for an instant at the top. Its weight still pulls, unbalanced. At rest, yet not in equilibrium.

V3.text: Your turn. A parachutist drifts down at a steady five metres per second. Is she in equilibrium? Pause and decide.

V4.text: Yes! Steady velocity, zero acceleration. The drag on her parachute balances her weight.

W2.text: A five kilogram lamp hangs from two wires, at thirty and sixty degrees to the ceiling. Find both tensions.

W3.text: The weight is five times nine point eight. Forty nine newtons.

W4.text: Sideways: T one cos thirty equals T two cos sixty. So T two is root three times T one.

W5.text: Upward: T one sine thirty, plus T two sine sixty, equals forty nine. So two T one equals forty nine.

W6.text: T one is twenty four point five newtons, and T two about forty two point four. The steeper wire carries more.

X2.text: Many students say each string holds half the weight. W over two.

X3.text: But only the upward parts share the weight. T is W over two sine theta. W over two holds only for strings hanging straight down.

E1.text: Where is this asked? In strings at angles, and in which forces can balance.

Q1.text: Exam level now. A two metre string joins two hooks one point two metres apart, at one height. A four kilogram bag hangs at its middle. g is ten. Find the tension. Pause and solve.

A1.text: The answer is B. Twenty five newtons.

A2.text: Each half is one metre, spanning zero point six metres sideways. So cos theta is zero point six, and sine theta, zero point eight.

A3.text: The weight is forty newtons. Two T sine theta equals forty.

A4.text: So T is forty over one point six. Twenty five newtons.

F1.text: Here is your recap. Screenshot this card.

Y1.text: Can you answer these without help?

Y2.text: One. Why can Aarav never pull his rope perfectly straight?

Y3.text: Two. Can forces of two, three and six newtons balance? Why?

Y4.text: Three. Is a ball at the top of its throw in equilibrium? Why?

N1.text: Next time: a magnet pulls a pin without touching it. How can a force cross empty space? Contact and non-contact forces.
